generatedProse.concept-context: In your subject, the same line applies. You can learn from AI, and use it where a brief allows, but you cannot submit its work as your own or hand in material it invented. A fabricated reference or a confidently wrong claim becomes your responsibility the moment you include it. If several of you lean on the same tool and prompt, your work can end up looking alike, which can count as collusion even when no one intended it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students using AI on the same assignment, where the brief sets Category 2.

{{learner-a}} asks a chatbot to write a section, pastes it in with light edits, and keeps a journal reference the tool supplied. The reference turns out not to exist, and the writing is the tool's, not {{learner-a}}'s. That is plagiarism and fabrication, and {{learner-a}} is responsible for both.

{{learner-b}} uses the chatbot to suggest an angle, then writes the section in their own words, finds and checks real sources, and adds a short statement of how AI was used. Nothing is passed off, and nothing is invented.

Both used AI on a task that allowed it. Only {{learner-a}} crossed the line into misconduct.
generatedProse.summary: Cardiff Met treats several AI-related behaviours as academic misconduct: plagiarism, commissioning, fabrication, collusion, substantial alteration, and using prohibited sources. The thread through all of them is that the work you submit must be your own, and you are responsible for anything in it, including any error or bias the tool introduced. Used within the category your brief sets, AI is fine; passing off its work, or handing in what it invented, is not. You can now recognise misconduct, tell it apart from allowed use, and see where your responsibility lies. The next lesson shows how to use AI honestly when a brief allows it, and how to declare it.

check.body: On an assignment in {{context}}, you paste an AI-written paragraph into your work and include a reference the AI gave you without checking it. Why is this misconduct?

items.text: You have submitted AI's work as your own and included an invented reference - plagiarism and fabrication.
It is not misconduct, because you edited a few words.
It is misconduct only if the reference happens to be wrong.
It is fine, as long as the tool you used was free.

feedback.correct: That's right. Passing off AI's writing is plagiarism, and an unchecked invented reference is fabrication.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The paragraph is the tool's work submitted as yours (plagiarism) and the reference is invented (fabrication).
